problem: Which of the following is equivalent to $\frac{1}{{tan}^{2}⁡x{sec}^{2}⁡x-{tan}^{4}⁡x+1}?$
worked_solution:
First, we recall the different forms of the secant-tangent Identity:

$$
\begin{aligned} & (1) & 1+{tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x \\  & (2) & {tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x-1 \\  & (3) & {sec}^{2}⁡x-{tan}^{2}⁡x=1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can rewrite our expression using $(3),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{{tan}^{2}⁡x{sec}^{2}⁡x-{tan}^{4}⁡x+1} & =\frac{1}{{tan}^{2}⁡x({sec}^{2}⁡x-{tan}^{2}⁡x)+1} \\  & =\frac{1}{{tan}^{2}⁡x\cdot 1+1} \\  & =\frac{1}{{tan}^{2}⁡x+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can use $(1),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{{tan}^{2}⁡x+1} & =\frac{1}{{sec}^{2}⁡x} \\  & ={(\frac{1}{\operatorname{sec}⁡x})}^{2} \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\frac{1}{{tan}^{2}⁡x{sec}^{2}⁡x-{tan}^{4}⁡x+1}={cos}^{2}⁡x.
$$
